title: Does wearing a glucose sensor and seeing your own readings help people at risk of type 2 diabetes improve their lifestyle choices?
official: Real-time contInuous glucose monitoring (RT-CGM) for behaviour-only glycaemic improvement in adults with dysglycaemia: a mixed methods pilot randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
Prediabetes means blood sugar (glucose) levels are higher than normal but not high enough to be diabetes. Up to 7 in 10 people with prediabetes go on to develop type 2 diabetes in their lifetime. A continuous glucose monitor (CGM) is a small sensor worn on the arm or tummy that measures glucose day and night and shows the readings on a phone or handset. CGMs help people who already have diabetes, but we do not know whether they help people with prediabetes. This study aims to find out whether being able to see your own glucose readings, without any formal diet plan, exercise programme or coaching, helps people make their own lifestyle changes and if these changes improve their glucose levels. It will also check whether a larger future study would be possible.

Who can participate?
Adults aged 18 or over with prediabetes (an HbA1c blood test result of 42–47 mmol/mol) who have not taken part in the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme. 

What does the study involve?
At the first visit, participants come in fasted for blood tests, body measurements, questionnaires and a glucose tolerance test. In this test they drink a sugary drink and have blood samples taken over 2 hours. They then wear a “blinded” glucose sensor for 10 days. It records glucose in the background but does not show any readings. Participants are then put at random into one of two groups. The sensor group wears a real-time Dexcom G7 sensor for 12 weeks and can see their readings at any time. Anything they do with this information is up to them. The comparison group carries on with usual care and wears another blinded sensor for 10 days at Week 10. For the 12 weeks, both groups use a step-counting app and complete a short online food diary twice a week. Everyone returns at Week 12 to repeat the first visit’s tests. People in the sensor group can choose to wear one more blinded sensor at about Week 20, to see whether any changes last, and may be invited to an online interview about their experience.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants receive a detailed assessment of their glucose and a set of blood tests. Those in the sensor group get access to a glucose sensor that is not currently available on the NHS for prediabetes. The possible risks are minor. The sensor can cause redness, itching or discomfort where it sits. Blood tests can cause bruising or faintness. The sugary drink can cause nausea or bloating. Some people may find watching their glucose readings worrying. The visits, app and food diaries take up some time.

Where is the study run from?
The University of Liverpool, with study visits at Aintree University Hospital, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
April 2027 to December 2028

Who is funding the study?
Dexcom

Who is the main contact?
Dr Matthew Anson, manson1@liverpool.ac.uk

interventions.name:
Participants are randomised 1:1 using computer-generated block randomisation with random permuted blocks of varying size, after a 10-day blinded CGM run-in (Weeks −2 to 0). Randomisation is carried out remotely and participants are told their allocation by telephone at Week 0.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Adults aged > = 18 years
2.	Prediabetes defined by a screening HbA1c of 42–47 mmol/mol (6.0–6.4%, DCCT) 
3.	Able and willing to give written informed consent
4.	Have not previously taken part in the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Clinical diagnosis of diabetes, including diabetes in remission
2.	Current use of metformin, incretin-based therapies (GLP-1 agonists, dual GLP-1/GIP agonists, 2 common brands are ‘Ozempic’ and ‘Mounjaro’) or other weight-loss pharmacotherapy, including agents taken privately 
3.	Current or recent use of glucocorticoids
4.	Planned or previous bariatric surgery
5.	Pregnancy
6.	Previous extensive use of RT-CGM (> = 4 sensors/past year)
7.	Current or anticipated treatment with hydroxyurea during the study period 
8.	Renal replacement therapy (haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis), or critical illness 
9.	Planned MRI or diathermy during sensor wear that cannot be rescheduled or accommodated by sensor removal 
10.	Known adhesive allergy, or dermatological condition, extensive scarring or tattooing at both approved insertion sites (abdomen and posterior upper arm) precluding sensor wear
